# Propositions Continued

## Parse Trees

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q 

```

Apply the outermost relevant rule...

::::: columns
::: {.column style="width: 50%; text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em; white-space: nowrap;"}
$((\text{Tu} \wedge \text{Th}) \wedge (\text{Sa} \vee \text{Su}))$
:::

::: {.column style="width: 50%; text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em; white-space: nowrap;"}
$(\text{Tu} \wedge (\text{Th} \wedge (\text{Sa} \vee \text{Su})))$
:::
:::::


::: notes
Work outward-in: the outermost parentheses are the last rule applied, so they
are the root. Each internal node is a rule application, each leaf an atom.

EXPECT THE QUESTION: "how do we know which operator goes with the outer
parentheses?" Answer by annotating, not by algorithm -- say outright that the
programmatic version waits for 221, and that for now this is observational.

Write the depth under each operator:

      ((Tu ^ Th) ^ (Sa v Su))          (Tu ^ (Th ^ (Sa v Su)))
          2       1     2                  1      2      3

Depths 2,1,2 -- the middle one is the root. Depths 1,2,3 -- the first one is.
Same symbols, different tree, visible without parsing anything.

Counting version, if they want to do it by hand: the root is the operator with
exactly ONE more "(" than ")" to its left. Same fact, two tallies instead of a
running counter.

Why it works is the grammar: ( <wff> op <wff> ) wraps every binary operator in
its OWN parentheses, so an operator's depth counts how many rule applications
deep it sits. Exactly one sits at depth 1.

Edge case, and someone will write it: ~<wff> adds no parentheses, so on
~(p ^ q) the counting rule points at the ^ when the root is the leading ~. Rule
of thumb -- if it starts with ~, that is the root; otherwise count.

The trees are **different** -- and every row of the truth table agrees. That gap
is the point. The parentheses fix the structure, the structure fixes how you
evaluate, but two structures can evaluate the same everywhere. What the
parentheses buy you is a definite answer, not a unique expression.

That is the opening for Monday: logical equivalence is exactly this relation --
different formulas, same truth table. Do not name it yet; just let them notice
that two different trees came out the same.
:::

## WFFs

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q 

```
Theorem: $\neg (p ∨ q))$ is not a WFF.

Proof:

::: notes
<!-- assume that it is! then ~<wff> must have been the last rule applied, 
and $( p v q))$ must be a <wff>. then ( <wff> v <wff> ) must have been the 
last rule applied, and $p$ and $q)$ must be <wff>. take each case separately:
$q)$ is not a <wff> because none of the rules apply, so we have both that it 
must be a wff and it is not a wff -- a contradiction, so our assumption 
is false!  

We include this as foreshadowing for a proof strategy called "proof by 
contradition."" Making arguments like this (proofs) is the substance of this course, 
but don't worry, we'll be teaching you how to do it. -->
:::



## Back to Propositions

A *proposition* is a statement that can be either **True** or **False**.

Examples:

-   $37 > 12$

-   Fewer than 5 people in this room feel sleepy.

-   There are extra-terrestrial life forms.

-   This statement is False.

-   $\underline{\hspace{10em}}$

## Translation

From English to logic and back...

\

$p$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ate cereal for breakfast.

$q$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ brought a backpack to class.

 

-   $(p\lor q)$

-   $(p\wedge q)$

-   $\neg q$

# Logical Equivalence

## Logical Equivalence

\

Ex: Is it true that $(p \lor q) \equiv (q\lor p)$ ?

Ex: Is it true that
$((\text{Tu} \wedge \text{Th}) \wedge (\text{Sa} \vee \text{Su})) \equiv (\text{Tu} \wedge (\text{Th} \wedge (\text{Sa} \vee \text{Su})))$ ?

\

Discussion points:

-   $\equiv$ means *logically equivalent*

-   The answer had better be \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_!!!

-   How can we justify our instinct?

::: notes
The blanks are in Identity, Domination and Negation. Identity and Negation hide
two cells each; Domination hides four, because both the operand and the result
are greyed on each of its lines. All eight are **T** or **F**, and all eight
follow from the $\wedge$ and $\vee$ truth tables -- no new vocabulary needed.

Spend the last bullet on **Negation**: $p \vee \neg p \equiv$ **T** and
$p \wedge \neg p \equiv$ **F** are tautology and contradiction. Filling those two
cells *is* the next slide; it only supplies the names.

De Morgan is two rows further down -- flag it, since the cereal slide verifies
it.
:::

## Special Logical Equivalences

Suppose $p\equiv$ **T** .
Then $p$ is a *Tautology*.

Suppose $p\equiv$ **F** .
Then $p$ is a *Contradiction*.

## Chains of Equivalence

\

$(((p \wedge q) \wedge r) \vee ((p \wedge q) \wedge \neg r))$

\

$\equiv$

\

$\equiv$

\

$\equiv$

::: notes
The other method. Truth tables settled the last one; this settles it by rewriting,
one named law at a time.

Three variables, so a truth table is 8 rows. The chain is 3 lines. Say that out
loud -- it is the whole argument for learning the laws.

  (((p ^ q) ^ r) v ((p ^ q) ^ ~r))
  == ((p ^ q) ^ (r v ~r))            Distributive
  == ((p ^ q) ^ T)                   Negation
  == (p ^ q)                         Identity

Every line is a WFF -- fully parenthesised, one binary operator per pair. Worth
being fussy about here, one slide after parse trees.

r vanishes. That is the point to sit on: r appears twice in the original and
cannot change the answer. They meet exactly this again in HW1.

This is also the thing Tutorial 1 asks for tomorrow, and this is the only worked
example they get before it.
:::
